analysis.investment_thesis: Marc Technocrats is a micro-cap fast grower posting 35–41% CAGR across revenue, EBITDA, and net profit with virtually zero debt and superb capital returns (ROCE 36%), fitting Lynch's classic "small company, big growth" profile. However, with no P/E or market cap data available, I cannot calculate a PEG ratio — and without valuation discipline, even the best growth story risks being a value trap at the wrong price.
key_strengths: 35–41% 3-year CAGR across all P&L lines — revenue nearly tripled from ₹19 Cr to ₹48 Cr in 3 years
Virtually debt-free (₹1 Cr total debt) with ROCE of 36.27% — this is a capital-light compounder
OCF positive all 4 years; 73.5% promoter holding signals strong owner-operator alignment
key_risks: No P/E or market cap data — PEG ratio is uncalculable, making GARP discipline impossible to apply
Operating CF (₹5 Cr) meaningfully lags net profit (₹7 Cr) in FY25 — earnings quality concern and possible receivables build-up
Extremely small revenue base (₹48 Cr) in consulting services makes the business fragile to client concentration and key-person risk
red_flags: Listed exchange shows 'YHD-ERR' — unclear or erroneous exchange listing raises liquidity and governance concerns
FII + DII ownership below 2% — near-zero institutional validation on this name
Investing CF (-₹4 Cr) exceeds disclosed capex (-₹3 Cr) — the unaccounted ₹1 Cr outflow needs explanation
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Marc Technocrats ticks every box on Lynch's fast-grower checklist in isolation: revenue compounding at 35%, net profit at 41%, ROCE of 36%, and a near-pristine balance sheet with ₹1 Cr debt against ₹28 Cr equity. For a consulting services outfit at this scale, margin expansion — EBITDA margins moving from ~21% in FY22 to ~23% in FY25 — suggests real operating leverage, not financial engineering. This is exactly the kind of unknown, under-followed micro-cap Lynch hunted in the early Magellan days.

That said, three things keep me from pounding the table. First and foremost, the absence of any valuation metric makes the PEG ratio — my single most important tool — impossible to apply. A stock growing 40% at a PEG of 0.5 is a ten-bagger; the same stock at a PEG of 3.0 is a disaster. Second, the OCF-to-net-profit gap (₹5 Cr vs ₹7 Cr) in FY25 hints at rising receivables, which in a consulting business could mean lumpy or deferred billing. Third, the 'YHD-ERR' exchange tag and near-zero institutional ownership are classic warning signs of illiquidity. I'll watch this name — the story is interesting — but I need a price before I can act.
